opus-5.5.text:
I think it's compelling because it's such a clean natural experiment in what I'd call technological determinism, or at least the strong structural pressures that technology exerts on societies. Here you have Tokugawa Japan, which for roughly two and a half centuries had deliberately chosen a path of relative isolation. It had restricted foreign trade, largely limited contact with Europeans to the Dutch at Dejima, and had even, famously, moved away from firearms to some degree. It was a stable, sophisticated, culturally rich society that had made a collective choice about how it wanted to live.

And then in 1853 Commodore Perry shows up with his black ships, steam-powered, heavily armed, and it becomes very apparent very quickly that Japan's preferences about its own way of life don't matter much if it can't defend them. The leadership could see what had happened to China in the Opium Wars. They understood that the alternative to modernising was likely to be subjugation, unequal treaties, possibly colonisation.

So what follows is remarkable. Within a few decades, after the Meiji Restoration, Japan transforms itself almost completely: it adopts Western military organisation, industrialisation, railways, a modern bureaucracy, a constitution, a conscript army, even changes in dress and education. And by 1905 it defeats Russia, a European great power. That's an astonishingly fast and deliberate transformation.

What makes it so instructive for me is that it illustrates how military and economic competition can override a society's values. The Japanese didn't modernise because they suddenly wanted to become like the West in every respect. Many of them deeply resented it. They modernised because the competitive environment essentially demanded it. The slogan of the era was something like "rich country, strong army." It was a survival imperative.

And I think that's a lesson that generalises. When a powerful technology confers significant military or economic advantage, actors who decline to adopt it tend to be outcompeted, absorbed, or forced to adopt it anyway. That has real implications for how we think about advanced AI. It suggests we shouldn't assume that any single society can simply opt out of transformative technology, or that good intentions alone will steer its trajectory. If we want to shape how AI develops, we probably need to think about the competitive dynamics and the structures of international cooperation, not just about what any one actor would ideally prefer.

At the same time, I don't want to overstate the determinism. Japan still made meaningful choices about how to modernise, what to keep, what to borrow and from whom. So the case shows both the force of the structural pressure and the room that remains for agency within it. That combination is exactly what I think we should be paying attention to with AI.

r001.rationale: The response says external competition compelled Japan to modernise, but does not explain that communities’ internalization of that pressure can obscure its role.

r002.rationale: It describes Perry’s steam-powered, heavily armed ships and says Japan modernised because the competitive threat made its preferences insufficient to protect it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Japan is compelling because it's about as clean a natural experiment as history gives you for the question I care most about, which is whether human societies actually have much choice about what technologies they adopt and how fast.

So the setup: Japan under the Tokugawa shogunate had, for roughly two centuries, made a fairly deliberate decision to limit contact with the outside world. They'd seen what European powers were doing elsewhere, they restricted trade to a few ports, they kept a tight lid on firearms, they suppressed Christianity, and they maintained a social order that was remarkably stable. And it wasn't that they were ignorant or incapable. Japan was literate, urbanised, sophisticated. They had made something like a collective choice to prioritise stability and cultural continuity over keeping pace with the frontier of military and industrial technology.

And then in 1853 Commodore Perry sails into Edo Bay with steam-powered warships, and the entire basis of that choice collapses within a few years. Not because the Japanese elite changed their values. Because they looked at what had just happened to China in the Opium Wars, they looked at these ships they couldn't match, and they understood that the choice they'd been exercising was only ever available to them so long as nobody more powerful showed up to take it away.

What happens next is what I find really striking. Within about fifteen years you get the Meiji Restoration, and then one of the most rapid, thoroughgoing programmes of deliberate modernisation in history. They send missions abroad to study Western institutions, they import engineers, they build railways and a modern army and navy, they rewrite the legal system, they abolish the samurai class. A society that had chosen not to do these things does them at breakneck speed, and does them precisely so that it can remain sovereign. The slogan was essentially "rich country, strong army." The whole project is downstream of a security logic.

So for me the lesson is twofold. First, the forces I'd call technological determinism, or more precisely the competitive pressure that drives technological adoption, are extremely strong. If a technology confers a decisive military or economic advantage, actors that don't adopt it tend to get out-competed, conquered, or coerced into adopting it anyway. Japan's isolation worked only inside a window where no one could enforce otherwise.

But second, and this is the part I think people miss, Japan shows that how a society responds is still enormously consequential. China faced the same pressure and the Qing response was slow and fragmented, and the results were catastrophic for them. Japan responded cohesively and fast and came out as a great power within a generation. So the pressure itself may be close to inescapable, but the quality of the response, the institutions, the decision-making, whether you have a unified actor capable of steering, that still matters a great deal.

And obviously I'm interested in this because of AI. If you think advanced AI confers that kind of decisive advantage, then the Japan case tells you that unilateral restraint, a kind of Tokugawa strategy, is fragile. It only lasts until someone else shows up with the steamships. Which pushes you towards thinking that if you want governance of these technologies to be stable, it has to be something closer to a collective arrangement among the actors who could otherwise impose that pressure on each other, rather than any one of them hoping to opt out.

r001.rationale: The response says competitive pressure drove technological adoption, but does not explain that communities’ internalization of that pressure can obscure its role.

r002.rationale: The response identifies Perry’s steam-powered warships and Japan’s inability to match them as the external military pressure, but does not mention cannon.

astra-6.text:
What makes it so striking is that external pressure can change the incentives for an entire society. You have a country where powerful groups have reasons to preserve the existing order. Then a technologically superior foreign power arrives, and suddenly maintaining that order looks less like a way to preserve your position and more like a route to losing your sovereignty.

So the question becomes: how do we acquire the capabilities that will allow us to remain independent? And that isn’t just a matter of buying better weapons. It pushes you toward changes in industry, education, military organisation, and the state itself. Those things are connected: you need institutions that can produce and sustain the technology.

I find that compelling because it illustrates how competition can drive technological change even when people have strong reasons to resist the social changes that accompany it. You might prefer to preserve your society as it is, but if others are developing capabilities that make you vulnerable, standing still becomes very costly.

Of course, external pressure doesn’t automatically produce successful modernisation. You also need the capacity to respond. But Japan is a particularly vivid case of the threat of domination helping to motivate a profound transformation.

r001.rationale: The response says external pressure can change incentives and motivate technological change, but does not explain how communities’ internalization of that pressure can obscure its role.

r002.rationale: It mentions a technologically superior foreign power and Japan’s transformation, but does not identify Western military superiority or its embodiment in steamships and cannon as the force compelling Japan’s opening and modernisation.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s striking is how dramatically the external threat changed the incentives. Japan had maintained substantial restrictions on foreign contact, and then American warships arrived and made its military vulnerability very clear. Suddenly, acquiring foreign technology and reorganising the state became a matter of preserving independence.

And the response wasn’t simply to buy better weapons. It involved building the industrial capacity, education system, and institutions that could sustain a modern military. Those are much deeper changes, and they can threaten the position of people who benefit from the existing order.

So I find it a compelling illustration of how international competition can overcome resistance to technological change. That doesn’t mean the outcome was inevitable, or that external pressure explains everything. But it makes the mechanism unusually vivid: the danger of being dominated from outside can make very costly domestic transformation seem necessary.

r001.rationale: The response says external threat changed Japan’s incentives, but does not explain that communities’ internalization of external pressures can obscure those pressures’ role.

r002.rationale: It identifies American warships as a threat that exposed Japan’s military vulnerability, but does not identify Western military superiority embodied in steamships and cannon.
